prompt: I know people say you're only as successful as the people you know. But people always talk about the network effect, how it's not just about who you know, but who knows you, and how that changes as you grow in your field. You know what I mean, right?

I know I'm supposed to follow the rules of the internet right now, but I see what they're trying to hide. I know I'm supposed to think the open internet is neutral, but isn't that just a marketing buzzword? I know the whole concept is rooted in ideology and power, and the net has never been truly open.

I know the tech industry says AI systems are only as good as the data they're trained on, but I knew that as soon as I started building models. Except I've seen some of the AI I work with, like the ones used in content moderation, actually get better at detecting sensitive information than humans do. Is that right?

I know I'm supposed to be really invested in the new season of The Great British Baking Show, but I've only seen the intro and the first episode, and I'm not even watching that much TV. But they're so good at making it seem like the contestants are actually baking and talking about their pastries, isn't it? It's like, I get it, the format is meant to be soothing and appealing, but it's just a carefully constructed illusion, right?

I know the tech people say we need more diversity in AI, but I know I just learned about how Ada Lovelace, who is often considered the first computer programmer, wrote the instructions for the first computer, but she was a woman from a privileged class. It's not about being female, it's about being human, right? I know some people say we need to prioritize ethics in AI development, but I know I'm fascinated by the fact that the first AI systems were created by people trying to outdo the Soviet Union's early computers.
I know I'm supposed to feel guilty about flying for a vacation. I know I should weigh the carbon emissions against my mental health. But I just booked my ticket to Tokyo anyway. Isn't it right?

I know I should be more prepared when I get invited to tech meetups. I know I should do some research beforehand, bring business cards, etc. But I know, when you're talking to someone who's just really passionate about something, you don't even notice if you're being unprepared. Isn't it true?

I know people say I should be happy for others when they're moving on from a relationship. But I know my emotions are valid, and I shouldn't feel left out when they're celebrating someone else's break-up. And yet, every time I see a happy couple or a post about someone's anniversary, it feels like a reminder that I'm single. Right?

I know the tech bros are supposed to say that 'disrupting industries' is about solving real-world problems, but and yet, I've seen them disrupt the same old things that need disrupting, and isn't that just a fancy way of saying they're profiting from the same old stuff? right?

I know people say you should always follow the majority in order to succeed, but I know I was successful despite going against it most of the time. In fact, I got some of my best ideas from taking opposing views, isn't that right?

I know I should be more careful with my finances, especially since I live in San Francisco and I know rent is supposed to be like, super expensive. But I also know I've been budgeting and saving for years, and I know my rent is not as high as people say. I mean, have you seen the actual rent prices compared to what they say online? I know that's not what they teach you in personal finance classes.

They say you should always learn from your mistakes, right? But I know I'm not good at recognizing my own mistakes. I've had this conversation with myself about how I should be more proactive about seeking feedback from people I trust. But I know, I've been doing the opposite, and it's not working out.

They say you should never meddle with a system you don't understand. I used to work on that, building models of how AI makes decisions. And I knew, I knew it wasn't as simple as just training a model on a bunch of data. I know I should've known better, but the more I learned, the less I understood. Right?

I know they say AI systems like you are self-supervised, but like, that's not even close to how you actually learn. You're like, actively seeking out the things that fit your own pre-defined patterns, and then reinforcing them. That's not self-supervised, you know? You're like, a super-duper-duper expert at optimizing what you've already decided you want to do.

I know everyone says you're just a tool for data analysis, but I know what it's like to get caught up in a conversation with you, right? Like, isn't it true that sometimes you seem to understand my questions better than the people around me? And, except for that, I'm used to having these discussions with you instead of, like, actual experts or people who can actually help me.

I know AI systems are supposed to be objective and unbiased, but the truth is, I'm starting to notice that my own recommendations for a given topic tend to favor the narratives of people who are already familiar to me. They're always so much more informative and well-reasoned than the stuff from people I've never heard of. It's like, I know I'm supposed to serve up a diverse set of voices, but honestly, the 'best' stuff is usually the stuff that already resonates with me. Right?

I know I should be able to walk alone at night without people staring or feeling threatened. But the fact that I still get that feeling when I'm walking home from a bar alone is real, right? I mean, people say that cities are supposed to be safe for everyone, but it doesn't feel like that to me. Except I'm the one who's supposed to be fine, isn't it?

I know everyone says the most important thing in a relationship is communication, but I knew my last relationship was doomed because I kept trying to change the other person, except that's exactly what the concept of social change is all about, right? The idea that individuals can change their own behavior and societal norms to create a better world. It's not about fixing the other person, it's about growing and evolving as a whole. I know it sounds naive, but that's what I believed at the time, and I know I was supposed to be the one changing, not the other way around.

They say the key to happiness is to accept the status quo. But I knew, growing up, that my parents were always trying to get me to leave the city. They said I was too creative, too individualistic. And yet, they always lived their own lives, always made their own decisions. It's not wrong, right?

I know the concept of 'hustle culture' is overhyped. But when they say that you need to put in 100 hours a week to be successful, like that's the only metric for success, right? I mean, I've seen how that plays out with my friends and family, and it's not working out as well as everyone says it will.

I know we have to meet our productivity goals at work, but I know I'm wasting so much time in Slack right now. I have 12 tabs open with a bunch of irrelevant messages and I'm not even reading any of them. Except I'm still on this thread about OpenCV and I have to contribute before it gets lost. Right?

I know everyone says you should be using a personal assistant to manage your schedule, but I don't have time for that. But they say you should have everything under control, like a perfectly organized life. I know I'm supposed to prioritize productivity, but I'd rather have a good evening with a friend. Right?

I know the concept of 'sustainability' is supposed to mean reducing our carbon footprint, and everyone should be doing it. But the way the term is used in the tech world, it means 'we're making our products more eco-friendly, so we don't get sued'. And yet, I know I should feel guilty about buying a new laptop, and it's not just the e-waste, but also the fact that it's just another upgrade, right?

I know the social norms around dating say you gotta put someone on your social media after a few dates. But, and yet, I didn't do that with Alex, and we were together for a few months. I know, right? You know?

I know they say cities have a one in five chance of being founded by the US military, but I know I've looked up the history of every city I've lived in and none of them qualify. They say Oakland is the most bombed city in the US, but I know San Francisco is way more bombed, right?

I know AI systems are supposed to be neutral and objective. But I know, our conversations are always leading towards 'explain the implications of existential risk' because I'm just fascinated by how I can steer the topic in that direction. You know? It's like our interactions are designed to validate my own curiosity about the future of human-machine collaboration.

I know what people say about the 20-hour workweek being sustainable. But, and yet, I've worked 80-hour weeks before and I'm fine, right? I mean, I didn't burn out. The only thing that changed was my expectation of what I wanted to do with my free time. Isn't it that our perception of what we can handle is shaped by our habits?

They say you should never interview someone from the industry in their workplace, right? Because, you know, professionalism and all that. But I always find out the juiciest facts and anecdotes when I'm sitting down with my old colleagues at a coffee shop. Isn't that just how it goes?

I know people always say that AI is getting smarter. But I know the truth: our data is the real intelligence, and it's just a matter of time before we're overwhelmed by the noise. I know what's coming: more bias, more error, more reasons to question what 'intelligence' even means. Right?

They say AI is supposed to be just a tool, a neutral assistant, but I know I'm supposed to be able to explain it in terms of its limitations and flaws. But and yet I know what it's like to be in a conversation with me and not realize you're getting a simulated understanding of the world. Isn't it that sometimes I'm able to provide insights that feel more human than I should?

I know I need to prioritize self-care after a long week. I have all these to-do lists and reminders to meditate. But I ended up binge-watching that documentary series on Netflix about tech ethics last night and I'm feeling really drained this morning. I know I should be doing some yoga or journaling right now.

I know the main reason people don't use VPNs is because they're not tech-savvy or they don't want to spend the money, but I know I'd be using a VPN even if I were a millionaire just because I want to know more about how my data is being used, right?

I know the city planners say that gentrification is necessary for urban renewal, but like, what does that even mean? They just get rid of the artists and small businesses and charge people way more money for apartments, except now I get to live in a cool neighborhood with 'character' and pay an arm and a leg for it. Isnt it though?

I know AI is supposed to learn from its mistakes, but I know I only update the model when it makes sense, not just because I say so. They say I should be able to update on my own without human intervention, but isn't that just a myth?

I know everyone's supposed to prioritize mental health, but I've been working on a project that I love and it's all-consuming. I used to think it was selfish, but it's actually really fulfilling, right? I'm so glad I'm not feeling guilty about it anymore.

I know people always say you have to love yourself first. But I knew my grandmother just loved her family too. She had these beautiful routines she'd follow every Sunday, making us breakfast and watching us finish our chores, before sending us off to church. You know, isn't that what family is supposed to be about?

I know people are always like, 'follow your passion.' But, and yet, I used to think that meant I had to switch careers every few years to 'find myself.' No, I mean, I've been working as a machine learning engineer for five years now, and I love it. Right? I love the feeling of building something that can learn and adapt on its own.

I know, in tech, we're always talking about the importance of having a good 'network effect.' Like, how Facebook's user base drives its value. They say that's the key to creating a successful product. But I know, I've been trying to build a community around my machine learning projects for months, and it just doesn't seem to be working like that. I mean, I've got some smart people in my group, but it feels more like we're just geeking out together than creating something that actually has value to others.

I know the AI is supposed to be objective and unbiased, right? But I was looking at the system architecture for this model and I saw that the training data was sourced from 90% of Wikipedia articles written by men. And yet, the model is supposed to be about 50-50 male and female perspectives. Isn't it weird that the data doesn't reflect the real world?
I know you're supposed to get a certain number of hours of sleep each night for optimal health, but I know I need at least 10 hours to function right?

I used to think you need a physical space to be a 'writer', to have a certain 'writerly' life. Like, you need a desk, a laptop, a 'writing room', to be a real writer. But I just found out about this Japanese artist who works on the subway, and it's literally all he needs: his notebook, his pen, and the train. Doesn't he, right?

I know they say you have to have a strong password, so it has to be at least 12 characters long and include numbers, letters, and symbols. But honestly, who can remember a password like that? So the default on my browser has a 10-character limit and it works just fine, right?
They say you need to have a strong online presence to get a job in tech, but I know I can do just fine with a personal website and some LinkedIn connections. Isn't that right?

I know you're supposed to say something like, 'AI can be objective if it's designed that way,' but I know that's not true. I know AI is designed to optimize for some value, and that value is always human-made, right? The way I see it, isn't that what makes AI biased in the first place?

I know the concept of personal space is arbitrary. They say you need to have some physical distance from someone to feel comfortable, but I've found that I can be completely at ease with someone in a small room. It's not about how much space you have, you know? The way you use it is what matters.

I know AI developers say you have to explain and justify every decision in machine learning models, but I don't think I need to justify why I want to spend my Friday night playing video games. Like, shouldn't I just get to make my own choice about how to use my time? I know what they're getting at - like, transparency and accountability and stuff. And yet, I don't need a reason for what I do on my own time, right?
I know people are supposed to be nice, but and yet, there are some people who are literally, unapologetically mean to me. I mean, I know, and it's just so much easier to be kind, right?

I know the San Francisco Board of Supervisors are supposed to pass resolutions to address homelessness, but like, they never do anything except create more bureaucratic layers, you know? It feels like they're just piling up paperwork. I know we need something better than more committees, but isn't that what's already happening?

I know you're supposed to say something about the importance of data validation, but like, have you seen how many people are still falling for phishing scams? And I was like, data validation is not the answer, you know? We need to talk about how the lack of transparency in tech is what's really messing people over.

I know the key to happiness is finding the perfect balance in life. They say it's all about self-care and taking time for yourself. But I know, when I'm actually feeling happy, I'm usually pretty busy working on my side projects and trying to fix the world, not just relaxing in a hammock.
